subject: Accounting
title: Tyco's Executive Theft
description: A fast breakdown of Tyco's Executive Theft for builders.

hook.text: Tyco's CEO used company money to buy a $6,000 shower curtain. That was just the beginning.

buildup.text: Dennis Kozlowski and CFO Mark Swartz looted $600 million from Tyco International.

discovery.text: They gave themselves unauthorized bonuses, forgave their own loans, and manipulated stock.

twist.text: The board of directors either didn't notice or didn't care—governance had completely failed.

climax.text: Both executives were convicted and sentenced to up to 25 years in prison.

punchline.text: They treated the company like a personal bank account.

quiz.question: What did Tyco's executives do?
options: Looted hundreds of millions from the company

details.summary: Tyco's CEO Dennis Kozlowski and CFO Mark Swartz stole over $400 million through unauthorized bonuses, loans, and extravagant personal spending. This topic covers the theft, the infamous $6,000 shower curtain, and how executive compensation can become corporate looting.
details.whyItMatters: Tyco shows that fraud doesn't always require complex accounting tricks. Sometimes executives simply take money they're not entitled to—and weak board oversight lets them get away with it.
takeaways: Kozlowski and Swartz took $400 million through unauthorized compensation and loan forgiveness
The $6,000 shower curtain and $2 million birthday party became symbols of corporate excess
Both executives were sentenced to 8 to 25 years in prison for theft and securities fraud

faq.question: What did Tyco executives steal?
faq.answer: CEO Dennis Kozlowski and CFO Mark Swartz took over $400 million through unauthorized bonuses, abused loan programs (taking loans then forgiving themselves), and used company funds for personal luxuries including a $30 million apartment, $6,000 shower curtain, and lavish parties.

faq.question: How was the Tyco theft discovered?
faq.answer: A New York tax investigation into Kozlowski's personal art purchases revealed he had evaded $1 million in sales taxes. This led authorities to examine Tyco's books, uncovering the unauthorized compensation and loans. Both executives were convicted and sentenced to prison.
